title: Two Simple Shifts to Make the Most of Intervention 2026
author: Katie Hatlestad
summary: Katie Hatlestad describes two systemic adjustments her Wisconsin district made in the third year of its reading law to get struggling readers into the right intervention sooner. The first is a change to the assessment calendar: re-screening intervention students in May, starting interventions in the first week of school, and pushing fall screening to October so that summer slide can be separated from real need. She plans to move the winter screening to mid-December to avoid winter-break loss and to allow earlier course correction. The second is an Intervention Alignment Tool built as a Google Form that walks teachers through the next logical data question, from oral reading fluency to nonsense word fluency to alphabet knowledge, and ends in an intervention suggestion. She argues that the combined changes let the screening-triggered work of diagnostics, parent reports and personal reading plans finish in a single week that coincides with conferences. The piece is a practical, school-level account that also shares the tool for others to copy.
points: Screening in October rather than September separates students who merely need a summer-slide boost from those who need intensive support and a personal reading plan.
Shifting the winter screening to mid-December avoids winter-break learning loss and gives an earlier chance to adjust interventions that show weak growth.
The Intervention Alignment Tool turns a heap of screening and diagnostic data into a step-by-step decision path ending in a matched intervention.
Linking the form to a spreadsheet yields a clean list of intervention groups at each grade level, with placement tests then setting the starting point.
Timing the post-screening paperwork for conference week made it easier to gather parent input and signatures in person.
quotes: Previously, we were creating plans for students who needed the cobwebs dusted, but didn’t require the level of support that a personal reading plan implies.

By screening students in October, we were able to differentiate between the students who just needed a little boost to get over the summer slide and those who actually needed additional, more intensive support.

Beginning the screening process triggers diagnostic testing, data reports to parents, and the creation of personal reading plans. We were able to complete all these tasks the week after screening, which happened to be the week of parent-teacher conferences.
Many of our students don’t have time to waste in an ill-suited intervention that is delivered for 6+ weeks, which can happen if we’re not focused on the right data.
For example, if accuracy on ORF is low, it will prompt you to answer questions about Nonsense Word Fluency. If NWF is low, it will take you to questions about Alphabet Knowledge.
From there, we can give the placement test for the chosen intervention to identify a starting point within the intervention.

Making these systemic adjustments helped us to meet state requirements more efficiently. But even more importantly, it ensured that our students were properly identified and given an intervention that would meet their needs.
